SCENE CONTEXT
One continuous shot, interior of a small cramped soviet-era kitchen, warm morning. A man plays dead at the breakfast table while his wife cooks at the stove behind him; he revives while her back is turned and drops dead again the moment she turns around.

FORMAT MODE
One continuous 8-second shot (oner), static locked camera, no cuts. The camera does not cut or move by itself. Diegetic sound only. 16:9, 24 fps.

OPTICS
MEDIUM-WIDE 29° from seated eye height at the table — both characters in frame at all times: the man large in the left foreground at the table, the wife smaller in the right background at the stove. Deep focus, everything sharp. No drift.

FIRST FRAME / BLOCKING
The man lies collapsed at the table in the left foreground (x ≈ 35%), torso slumped over the tabletop, right cheek flat on the oilcloth, face toward the camera, one arm hanging off the table edge — dead state: green skin, X eyes, tongue out. The wife stands at the stove in the right background (x ≈ 70%), back to the camera, stirring the pan with a spatula, weight on one leg.

ACTION TIMING
0.0–1.5s — hold: he lies motionless, dead; she stirs the pan, steam rises; the faucet drips slowly.
1.5–2.0s — his near eye cracks half-open: the black X unfolds into a narrow watching eye, the pupil slides toward her back. The rest of him stays limp.
2.0–3.5s — seeing her back turned, he slowly and carefully straightens up to sitting, long spine unrolling, rope arms lagging behind and settling late; as he rises, the color of life flows down him from the head: the chartreuse skin turns warm terracotta, the olive hair and mustache turn wine-red, the mint t-shirt turns white with navy stripes, the tongue slips back under the mustache, both eyes open round and content.

— Edges: wobbly asymmetric hand-painted contours, never mechanically clean, never a smooth vector line; the paint occasionally slips a hair past its own contour.
— Shading: flat hard-edged painted shadow shapes, baked INTO the artwork itself — two or three tones per surface at most, no soft gradients, no blending, no airbrush, no roundness, no sculpted form.
— Accents: rough black ink scribble marks in the creases — elbow, hem, knee of the trousers, the folds of the t-shirt.
— Contours are dark matte paint strokes only: no glowing outline, no mint or coloured rim, no halo, no bevel, no drop shadow around the drawings.
— The characters are OUTSIDE the lighting system of the room. The window light does not exist for them: no highlights, no rim light, no cast light, no colour temperature shift, no darkening when they pass the dark doorway, no brightening in the sunlit patch. Their painted colours stay pixel-constant from the first frame to the last.
— Zero 3D on the characters: no CGI shading, no volumetric light, no subsurface scattering, no plastic sheen, no photorealism.

THE BACKGROUND IS A CLEAN STYLIZED CGI CARTOON RENDER and keeps its own light: chunky simplified geometry, smooth subdivision surfaces, soft rounded bevels on every edge, matte toy materials with a subtle sheen, soft raytraced shadows, gentle ambient occlusion in the corners, no photorealistic grime, no PBR realism.

— Texture: visible dry-brush grain inside every fill, faint paper tooth showing through, tiny gaps where the brush skipped. The texture is part of the drawing and stays identical in every frame.
— Edges: wobbly asymmetric hand-painted contours, never mechanically clean, never a smooth vector line; the paint occasionally slips a hair past its own contour.
— Shading: flat hard-edged painted shadow shapes, baked INTO the artwork itself — two or three tones per surface at most, no soft gradients, no blending, no airbrush, no roundness, no sculpted form.
— Her dress is ONE flat painted shape hanging straight from the shoulders — a simple silhouette with no folds modelled inside it, no fabric volume, no draping, no hip or thigh shapes showing through. Her legs below the hem are two simple flat painted shapes, and her feet in the slides are flat shapes too — no muscle, no knee joint modelling, no rounding.
— Accents: rough black ink scribble marks in the creases — elbow, hem, the folds of his t-shirt.
— Contours are dark matte paint strokes only: no glowing outline, no coloured rim, no halo, no bevel, no drop shadow around the drawings.
— The characters are OUTSIDE the lighting system of the room. The window light does not exist for them: no highlights, no rim light, no cast light, no colour temperature shift, no darkening when they pass the dark doorway, no brightening in the sunlit patch. Their painted colours stay pixel-constant from the first frame to the last.
— Zero 3D on the characters: no CGI shading, no volumetric light, no subsurface scattering, no plastic sheen, no photorealism.

THE BACKGROUND IS A CLEAN STYLIZED CGI CARTOON RENDER and keeps its own light: chunky simplified geometry, smooth subdivision surfaces, soft rounded bevels on every edge, matte toy materials with a subtle sheen, soft raytraced shadows, gentle ambient occlusion in the corners, no photorealistic grime, no PBR realism.

MOTION IS DRAWN, NOT SIMULATED: stepped limited animation on twos — clear held poses connected by short eased moves; every change of pose reads as swapping one flat drawing for the next flat drawing, never as a form turning in space. Between beats the poses hold completely still.

THE ARRANGEMENT, as the cut-out shows it
The wife stands facing camera, cut at the hips by the sink rim, her dark ink-navy topknot up, loose strands down her face, her brows raised, her eyes lowered, her mouth flat, her brick red-brown dress with its faint pattern. Both her arms hang down in front of her into the basin, wrists relaxed, digits held together and softly curled.
The husband stands close behind her and to her RIGHT, nearer to camera than she is. Her body covers most of him: what shows is his right shoulder and sleeve past her on the right, and his head. His head is tipped over towards her, temple against temple, and it OVERLAPS the right edge of her topknot with the two heads touching and no background showing between them. His eyes are half-lidded and aimed down and to the LEFT at her face. Terracotta skin, ginger hair standing up, dark ginger moustache, white t-shirt with navy stripes and black brush-marks on the sleeve.
Both his forearms come round her front and lie ON TOP of her dress, one lower and one a little higher, his hands resting on her with their digits held together.

This sheet holds no body, no pose and no clothes for this shot. It is a paint pot and an eye chart, used for the middle stretch of the shot and put away again.

COLOUR TIMELINE — THE THREE STATES, IN ORDER

FIRST STATE, FROM THE OPENING. He is ALL DEAD: flat chartreuse green skin, olive hair, olive moustache, GREEN stripes on his pale mint t-shirt, aubergine trousers, blue slippers, two black X marks for eyes, a small wine-red tongue out of his mouth.
SECOND STATE, THE MIDDLE OF THE SHOT. His head and his bare forearms come alive: face, scalp and forearms warm terracotta, hair and moustache ginger, eyes open with round dark pupils. HIS T-SHIRT KEEPS ITS GREEN STRIPES and his trousers stay aubergine right through this stretch — only his head and his forearms are alive.
THIRD STATE, FROM HIS SECOND DEATH TO THE LAST FRAME. He is ALL DEAD AGAIN and he stays that way. His face, his scalp and his forearms go back to flat chartreuse green, his hair and moustache back to olive, two black X marks in place of his eyes, the wine-red tongue back out of his mouth.
THE THIRD STATE HOLDS THROUGH EVERYTHING THAT FOLLOWS IT. He is green while he holds still. He is green while he falls. He is green when his head hits the radiator. He is green while his arms and legs land. He is green in the final arrangement, and he is green in the very last frame of the shot — exactly the colour he was in the very first frame. No terracotta comes back into him at any point after his second death, and moving does not change his colour.

HOW BIG HE IS IN THE FRAME

HE IS BIG. He is the largest thing in the picture and he dominates it.
Measured against the room: EACH OF HIS BLUE SLIPPERS IS AS BIG AS THE YELLOW BUCKET standing by the cabinets. HIS SHOULDERS ARE AS WIDE AS THE RADIATOR IS TALL. His head is as wide as three ribs of the radiator side by side.
Measured against the frame: from the crown of his head down to the tips of his slippers HE RUNS FROM THE RADIATOR ALL THE WAY DOWN TO THE BOTTOM EDGE OF THE PICTURE, his slippers coming right down to that edge and just touching it. HIS TWO HANDS, FLUNG OUT TO THE SIDES, REACH ALMOST TO THE TWO SIDE EDGES OF THE PICTURE, one out past the bucket and one out over the rug. He is the whole middle of the frame and there is little bare floor left around him.

HE IS A TALL GANGLY MAN, AND THE DRAWING HAS TO SAY SO

He is long-boned and loosely put together: a small head, a long thin neck, narrow sloping shoulders, a shortish body and very long limbs. Nothing about him is squat, stocky, chubby or short-limbed, and his head is small against the rest of him.
HIS PROPORTIONS, AS A CHECKABLE THING: measure from his hip to the tip of his slipper, and measure from his hip to the crown of his head. THE FIRST IS HALF AS LONG AGAIN AS THE SECOND. His legs take up the lower half of his whole length on screen. Each arm, from shoulder to fingertips, reaches as far as from his shoulder to his knee.
HIS NECK IS LONG. Between the collar of his t-shirt and his jaw there is a clear run of bare neck, as long as his head is tall, and it stays that long.

WHERE HIS HEAD IS — HE IS LYING WITH HIS HEAD AGAINST THE RADIATOR

HIS HEAD RESTS RIGHT UP AGAINST THE RIBBED RADIATOR. The crown of his head touches the lower ribs of it, and his mop of hair is spread out flat against those ribs in separate dark strokes, some of the strokes lying across the metal. THERE IS NO STRIP OF FLOOR SHOWING BETWEEN HIS HAIR AND THE RADIATOR: the two shapes meet. That contact is there in the very first frame and it is the anchor of the whole pose.

HOW HE LIES — READ THIS SLOWLY

He lies FLAT ON HIS BACK on the herringbone parquet, his head against the radiator, his body running out from it down the picture, one arm out past the bucket and the other out over the rug.
HE LIES AWAY FROM CAMERA, HEAD FURTHEST, FEET NEAREST. His head is up in the picture at the radiator, his shoulders below it, his hips below those, his knees below those and his slippers down at the bottom edge.
THE FORESHORTENING IS DRAWN INTO HIM AND IT IS STRONG. HIS TWO BLUE SLIPPERS ARE THE BIGGEST THING ABOUT HIM ON SCREEN. HIS HEAD IS THE SMALLEST THING ABOUT HIM. Between them everything grades: his hips read bigger than his shoulders, his knees bigger than his elbows, his slippers biggest of all. This gradient is painted into the drawing and stays exactly the same in every frame.

HIS HEAD. It lies tipped back against the radiator and ROLLED OVER TOWARDS THE SCREEN-RIGHT SIDE, so his face is turned up and off to that side. One big round ear shows on the SCREEN-LEFT side of his head. His long nose and his heavy moustache point off towards screen right. The two black X marks sit high on his face. TWO SEPARATE PAINTED EYEBROW STROKES sit above them, level and slack. The small wine-red tongue hangs out of the screen-right corner of his mouth and points down.

HIS NECK AND SHOULDERS. From his jaw the long neck runs DOWN AND TOWARDS SCREEN LEFT into the collar of his t-shirt. His shoulders are below and to either side of that collar, narrow and sloping.

HIS BODY. The pale mint t-shirt with its stripes lies across him, seen from above, so it reads WIDER THAN IT IS TALL — a broad soft shape with the stripes running across it. It is loose on him and rucked up a little at the hem, and a strip of aubergine shows below the hem before his trousers start. There are a few black ink scribble strokes at the shoulder seams and at the rolled cuffs of the short sleeves.

HIS ARMS. BOTH ARMS ARE FLUNG OUT AND DOWN, away from his body at about forty-five degrees, one to each side, like the two upper strokes of a letter X. Each is a short sleeve at the shoulder and then a LONG bare forearm running out and down. His two hands come to rest well out to the sides, level with his hips, lying open on the boards with the digits loose and apart. His arms hang there slack, without a bend of effort in them.

HIS LEGS. BOTH LEGS SPREAD DOWN AND OUT IN A WIDE V, one towards the bottom SCREEN-LEFT and one towards the bottom SCREEN-RIGHT, straight and slack, and they are LONG — the longest thing about him. The aubergine trousers run their whole length with a thin magenta line down the outside of each leg and black ink scribbles at the knees and the cuffs. Below the cuffs, a stretch of bare ankle on each side, and then the slippers.

HIS SLIPPERS. Two big deep-blue slippers, soft and rounded, one on each foot, BOTH FALLEN OUTWARD so their soles turn away from each other and their toes point out to the two bottom corners of the picture. Each has a few black ink strokes across its top. They are the nearest part of him to camera and the largest part of him on screen, and they come right down to the bottom edge of the frame.

WHAT THE WATER DOES ALL THE WAY THROUGH

The painted fountain over the brass fitting plays at the same strength from the first frame to the last, holding its own height and its own width the whole time. Its splayed crown keeps its overall silhouette and its size while the flat white shapes inside that silhouette reshape and jostle; small flat chips of white and blue pop off it into the air, hang for a moment and vanish, and new ones pop in their places; the blue band running down from it into the basin keeps the same width and the same length while its torn edges shift.
In the basin, the foam sits at its full amount from the very first frame: white clusters around the sides of the bowl with a patch of flat blue showing between them. THE BUBBLES POP AND COME BACK — small flat white bubble shapes burst and vanish, and new ones appear in their places, so the surface keeps working while the amount of foam stays the same. The water level in the basin stays exactly where it is. The counter, the cabinets and the parquet stay dry.
All of that water is drawn in two tones: solid muted mid-blue bodies filled flat and evenly, with separate flat white shapes laid on top and along their edges as crest, foam, bubbles and flecks. The edges are torn into soft tongues. The loose chips in the air are separate flat pieces of their own. It steps on twos.

TIMING

0.0 to 5.0 — HE IS DEAD AND THE WATER LIVES. He lies there splayed, green, his head against the radiator, and every part of him holds completely still: not a digit, not a drift, not a breath. Both X marks in place, the tongue hanging out. The fountain plays and the bubbles pop in the basin. That is the whole of the first five seconds.
5.0 to 5.6 — HIS HEAD COMES BACK. The terracotta runs into his face and up over his scalp, his hair and his moustache turn ginger, and the two X marks are replaced by living eyes with round dark pupils under soft painted lids. It arrives as one wave crossing his head. The tongue draws back into his mouth. His t-shirt keeps its green stripes and his trousers stay aubergine. He is still lying flat and has not moved yet.
5.6 to 6.0 — the terracotta carries on down both arms and reaches his hands, and it stops there. His arms stay where they lie.
6.0 to 6.6 — HELD. A living head on a dead green body, flat on the boards, eyes open, pupils low. The water plays.
6.6 to 7.6 — HE COMES UP ONTO HIS ELBOWS, A SMALL WAY ONLY, EVENLY AND WITHOUT HURRY. His forearms slide in under him and his elbows gather in towards his sides; his upper body hinges up at the hips, so HIS HEAD AND HIS SHOULDERS TRAVEL A SHORT WAY DOWN THE PICTURE, towards the camera and away from the radiator, and A STRIP OF PARQUET OPENS UP BETWEEN HIS HAIR AND THE RADIATOR RIBS. His hips, his legs and his slippers stay exactly where they are on the floor, still spread in their wide V. It is a small lift: his shoulders come up off the boards and no further. His head rolls level as he comes up, so his face turns towards the bottom of the picture. AS HE RISES HIS TWO EYEBROWS GO UP and his eyes open wider, so he arrives at the top of the move already expecting to see somebody. Every part of him keeps the same size on screen that it had lying down.
7.6 to 8.3 — HE LOOKS FOR WHOEVER IS SUPPOSED TO BE WATCHING. His pupils travel across to the SCREEN-LEFT side of his eyes and DOWN into the bottom left corner of the picture, off past the stove and the bucket towards the hallway, and settle there. His brows stay up. He holds it, waiting.
8.3 to 8.8 — NOBODY IS THERE, AND IT PUZZLES HIM. THE INNER ENDS OF HIS TWO EYEBROWS LIFT and the outer ends drop, so the two strokes make a soft peak over his eyes — the shape of a man who has been let down rather than a man who is cross. His lids come halfway down. His mouth goes small and pursed under the moustache. He blinks once, slowly, and his eyes come back to the same corner. Nothing else about him moves at all. The change is all in the brows, the lids and the mouth, as separate flat painted shapes sliding on his fixed painted face.
8.8 to 9.35 — HE HOLDS IT, propped on his elbows, brows peaked, mouth small, pupils still aimed off into the bottom left corner. Soft and quietly put out, a little hurt and a little bewildered. Nothing about him moves. The fountain plays and the bubbles pop.
9.35 to 9.5 — A SMALL FRIGHT. Something over in that corner catches him. HIS TWO EYEBROWS SHOOT UP, both of them, and his eyes go round and wide, the pupils shrinking to two small dots in the middle of them. His shoulders pull up short towards his ears and his mouth opens a little. It is a light startle, quick and small — a man caught doing something he should not be doing. He holds it for one exposed frame with the fright on his face.
9.5 to 9.65 — HE PLAYS DEAD ON THE SPOT. His eyes are replaced by the two black X marks, his brows go slack and level, the wine-red tongue drops out of the corner of his mouth. The terracotta goes out of his face, his scalp and his forearms and they are flat chartreuse green again, his hair and moustache olive again. Two exposed frames, quick and hard, arriving at full speed. HE HAS NOT MOVED HIS BODY AT ALL: he is still propped up on his elbows, in the exact same pose, just green.
9.65 to 10.1 — HELD, GREEN, STILL PROPPED. He stays exactly as he was, up on his elbows, X marks in place, tongue out, arms and legs unmoved — and completely green from his hair to his slippers. Absolutely nothing about him moves for this whole beat. A green corpse holding itself up on its elbows. This green pose is the pose everything after it comes from.
10.1 to 10.3 — HE FALLS BACKWARD AND HIS HEAD HITS THE RADIATOR. His elbows give out from under him and his whole upper body drops back and up the picture, gathering speed, with nothing catching it. THE CROWN OF HIS HEAD ARRIVES AGAINST THE RADIATOR RIBS AND STOPS DEAD ON ONE FRAME, hair flattening against the metal. His limbs are still flying at that moment. Three exposed frames: propped, halfway back with his arms already thrown, landed. HE IS GREEN THROUGH ALL THREE, the same green he was a moment before, with the X marks and the tongue.
10.3 to 10.5 — HE ARRIVES IN AN ABSURD ARRANGEMENT, AND NOTHING ABOUT IT MATCHES. THE SCREEN-LEFT ARM is thrown right back past his head, straight and long, the hand landing open against the ribs of the radiator above his hair. THE SCREEN-RIGHT ARM is folded across his chest, the hand come to rest up on his opposite shoulder. THE SCREEN-RIGHT LEG is bent, the knee up in the air and fallen inward so it crosses over the other thigh. THE SCREEN-LEFT LEG is thrown straight out and away at full length towards the bottom corner. His back is arched so his chest lifts off the boards and his shoulders press back. His head is rolled hard over to the SCREEN-RIGHT with the chin up and the tongue hanging out sideways. THE SLIPPER ON THE STRAIGHT LEG IS HALF OFF, hanging on the toes at an angle with the heel in the air. It is a body that landed however it landed, lopsided and ridiculous, and every limb is doing something different from every other. HIS SKIN, HIS HAIR AND HIS MOUSTACHE ARE THE SAME GREEN AND OLIVE THEY WERE BEFORE HE FELL.
Two frames after his head lands, the loose things arrive and settle last: his hair strokes, his hanging tongue and the half-off slipper.
10.5 to 15.0 — HELD to the last frame. He lies in that arrangement, GREEN, without a movement of any kind: chartreuse skin, olive hair and moustache, X marks in place, tongue out sideways, one arm back on the radiator, one folded on his chest, one knee up and fallen in, one leg out straight with the slipper hanging off it. The fountain goes on playing at the same strength, the chips popping off it and vanishing, the bubbles bursting and coming back in the basin. Everything else in the frame holds completely still.

RIGID PARTS

He is a flat painted cut-out lying on top of the rendered floor, and every part of him keeps its own size, its own length, its own width and its own painted texture from the first frame to the last. HIS PROPORTIONS AND HIS SIZE ON SCREEN ARE THE SAME IN EVERY FRAME: the same small head, the same long neck, the same long arms, the same long legs, the same big slippers, the same reach across the picture, and the same drawn foreshortening from small head to big slippers. His head keeps one outline and one size on screen in every frame — flat against the radiator, propped on his elbows, and in the final arrangement alike. His head, his neck and his shoulders are one connected painted shape at a fixed distance from each other throughout. His upper arms, forearms and hands are flat painted shapes turning at the shoulder, the elbow and the wrist, each keeping its length and its width, and each hand keeps FOUR digits and the quiet size it has in the first frame. His thighs, shins and feet are the same, turning at the hip, the knee and the ankle, and his legs keep their full length in every pose, the bent knee as long as the straight one. His eyebrows, his lids, his pupils, his moustache and his tongue are separate flat painted shapes that slide and turn on his fixed painted face, each holding its own shape. HIS COLOUR IS A SEPARATE THING FROM HIS MOVEMENT: whatever state he is in when a movement begins, he is in that same state throughout it and at the end of it. All of his movement stays in the flat plane of the picture. Depth is carried by the drawn foreshortening and by overlap rather than by any change of size. His painted shadows are permanent graphic shapes attached to the artwork and stay identical.

HOW THE ROOM IS RENDERED

The room stays a clean stylized CGI cartoon render: even surfaces, soft rounded bevels, matte toy materials, gentle raytraced shadows, and soft wide gradients across the walls, the parquet and the tiles.
THE ROOM KEEPS EXACTLY THE TONE OF THE PLATE. The same lightness, the same gentle contrast, the same colour. Darks stay soft grey-violet and keep their detail, highlights stay pale and keep theirs, the mid tones stay where they are, and every surface stays smooth and clean, with the same softness edge to edge. The whole frame keeps one even, calm, low-contrast look from the first frame to the last.
Brush texture, paint grain and hand-drawn contour belong to the painted man and to the painted water. Every surface of the room stays smooth.

EVERYTHING ELSE IS FROZEN

The stove, the kettle, the tiles, the sink, the brass fitting, the countertop, the dish rack and its plates, the cabinets, the bucket, the walls, the window, the curtain, the flowerpot, the radiator, the table, the oilcloth, the rug and the parquet all stay exactly where they are, at the same size and in the same shape, from the first frame to the last. The radiator holds its place and its shape when his head lands against it. The camera holds one fixed position, with no zoom, no pan, no tilt, no reframing and no focus pull, and the framing at the last frame matches the first, edge for edge.

MOTION LANGUAGE

A long thin dead man lies splayed across the kitchen floor, filling it, his head against the radiator, while a broken tap plays into the sink. His head comes back to life. He props himself up on his elbows and looks off towards the hallway for whoever is supposed to be watching, finds nobody there, and is quietly put out about it. Then something startles him, he goes green on the spot and holds it, and only after that do his elbows give: he drops back, cracks his head on the radiator and ends up in a completely ridiculous green heap. The water carries on. Stepped limited 2D animation on twos at 12 frames per second, pose-to-pose, long held poses and few drawings between them.

The shot opens on exactly this image, edge for edge: the same camera, the same looking-down angle, the same crop, the same light, the same colours, the room and everything in it in the same place, the painted fountain playing over the brass fitting, and THE GREEN MAN LYING ON THE PARQUET EXACTLY AS THIS IMAGE HAS HIM — his outline, his proportions, his colours, and his lopsided arrangement with one arm thrown back on the radiator, one folded on his chest, one knee up and fallen in, one leg straight out with the slipper half off. That is his pose and his drawing for every frame of this shot. Static locked camera on this framing, held to the last frame, 4:3.

WHAT THIS SHOT IS

A tap that nobody is going to turn off. The pouring is already running before the first frame and it is the same at the end as at the beginning. What changes is how high the water stands in the sink and how much of the floor is under it, and he lies there green and dead through all of it.

THE WATER IS DRAWN, NOT SIMULATED — READ THIS FIRST

Every bit of water in this picture is a HAND-PAINTED SHAPE CUT OUT OF PAPER AND LAID ON THE RENDER, in the same gouache, on the same paper, with the same brush as the man. It is not a substance and it does not behave like one.
THE WATER IN THIS SHOT IS A COUNTABLE SET OF SEPARATE FLAT SHAPES, and they are listed below one by one. Each one has its own outline, its own place and its own job. THEY NEVER MERGE INTO ONE CONTINUOUS MASS: where two of them meet there are two edges, plainly visible, the same as where his forearm meets his sleeve.
EVERY BLUE SHAPE is one solid muted mid-blue, filled flat and evenly edge to edge, one tone all through, with a torn dry-brush outline of hard little tongues. Nothing inside a blue shape is lighter or darker than the rest of it.
EVERY WHITE IS ITS OWN SEPARATE FLAT OPAQUE SHAPE laid on top of a blue shape or along its edge. White is never a shine or a highlight inside the blue: it is a piece of white paper sitting on top of a piece of blue paper.
NOTHING ABOUT THE WATER IS SEE-THROUGH. Nothing about it glints, sparkles or catches the light. Nothing in the room reflects in it. It shows no depth, no thickness and no rounding: it is flat colour with a cut edge.
IT MOVES AS A SMALL NUMBER OF HELD DRAWINGS. Each drawing sits still on screen, then the next drawing replaces it on one frame with nothing drawn in between. It is a sequence of separate pictures, on twos, not a continuous flow.

THE FOUR PIECES OF WATER, AND WHAT EACH ONE IS

ONE — THE FOUNTAIN over the brass fitting. One tall blue shape standing up out of the fitting, widening towards its top into a splayed crown, with a handful of separate white shapes laid across the crown and a few loose flat chips of white and blue hanging in the air beside it, each chip its own unconnected piece. It keeps the same height and the same width in every frame. Only the white shapes inside its silhouette swap for other white shapes, and the loose chips vanish and are replaced by other chips.

TWO — THE SHEET GOING OVER THE SINK RIM, AND IT REACHES THE FLOOR.
One long flat blue band that starts at the near edge of the sink and ENDS ON THE FLOOR. It is joined at the top to the blue in the basin, it runs down the whole front of the cabinet below, and at the bottom it meets the pool lying on the boards. THE TOP OF IT TOUCHES THE SINK RIM AND THE BOTTOM OF IT TOUCHES THE FLOOR, with no gap at either end and no free-hanging tip anywhere along it.
It is one even width along its whole length, from the rim right down to the boards, with a torn edge down each side and a few separate white flecks laid on it. Down at the bottom, where it meets the pool, it opens out a little wider and its edge tears into the shape of the pool.
IT IS ONE SHAPE AND IT KEEPS ITS SHAPE: the same width, the same length, the same place in every frame. Only its torn side edges swap for other torn edges. It never narrows, never breaks into pieces and never gathers into a drip or a blob at its lower end.

THREE — THE BLUE IN THE BASIN, AND IT RISES.
One flat blue shape filling the bowl, with the white foam clusters as separate white shapes sitting on top of it.
IT IS LOW AT THE START AND HIGHER AT THE END, and it comes up in steps together with the pool on the floor: at the beginning it sits a little below the rim of the sink; then it is level with the rim; then it stands slightly proud of it, humped a fraction above the edge, so that the sheet going over is plainly coming from a bowl that has more in it than it can hold.
Each of those levels is a HELD DRAWING that sits still on screen, and the next one replaces it in a single step, in the same rhythm as the pool. The foam clusters ride up with it and stay crowded on its surface.

FOUR — THE POOL ON THE FLOOR. One flat blue shape lying on the parquet, with a torn leading edge and a ragged line of separate white flecks laid along that edge. It is a piece of blue paper lying on the boards.

HOW THE POOL GROWS — SEPARATE HELD SHAPES, NOT A CREEPING LIQUID

The pool is redrawn a few times across the shot, and each redraw is A BIGGER PIECE OF BLUE PAPER THAN THE ONE BEFORE, covering more of the floor.
Each of those shapes is HELD STILL on screen for a stretch of time, and then the next, larger one replaces it in a single step. Between one shape and the next nothing is drawn: the edge does not travel, it is simply somewhere further out on the next held drawing.
Each new shape CONTAINS THE WHOLE OF THE ONE BEFORE IT: the floor that was blue stays blue, and only the outline reaches further.
The shapes in order cover: the boards at the foot of the cabinet; then out across the herringbone parquet; then round the yellow bucket, closing on both sides so the bucket stands in the blue; then up to the big blue slipper on his straight leg; then around both his slippers and along the hem of his trousers, with white flecks where the blue meets his painted shapes.
IN THE LAST FRAME THE POOL IS AT ITS BIGGEST AND THE TAP IS STILL POURING. The picture ends in the middle of the flood with no sign of it easing.

THE POURING NEVER LETS UP, AND THE WHOLE CHAIN RISES TOGETHER

The fountain over the brass fitting plays at exactly the same height and the same width in the last frame as in the first: as much water comes in at the end as at the beginning.
THE BLUE IN THE BASIN, THE SHEET DOWN THE CABINET AND THE POOL ON THE FLOOR ALL STEP UP TOGETHER, in the same rhythm and on the same held drawings. When the pool is redrawn bigger, the blue in the basin is redrawn higher on that same frame, and the sheet stays joined to both of them.
So the chain always reads whole, in this order from top to bottom: the fountain, the bowl brimming over, the sheet down the cabinet front, the pool on the floor. Each one touches the next.
Everything is already running before the first frame, and nothing about it eases off by the last.

HE DOES NOT MOVE, AND THAT IS THE JOKE

He holds the exact drawing he has in the first frame, from the first frame to the last: the same lopsided arrangement, the same limbs in the same places, the same flat chartreuse green skin, olive hair and moustache, the two black X marks, the wine-red tongue hanging out sideways, the half-off slipper hanging on his toes. Not a digit moves, not a shrug, not a breath, not a twitch when the water arrives. He is a painted cut-out lying on the floor and the flood happens around him.
He keeps the same size on screen and the same painted surface throughout. His painted shadows are fixed graphic shapes attached to the artwork.

WHAT ENDS UP UNDER THE BLUE AND WHAT STAYS CLEAR

Under the blue: the front of the cabinet under the sink, the boards of the kitchen floor, the rug, the foot of the bucket, and the lower parts of his slippers and trousers.
Clear of it: the counter top, the tiles, the stove, the kettle, the dish rack and its plates, the window, the flowerpot, the radiator, the table and its oilcloth.

THE ROOM IS THE ONLY RENDERED THING IN THIS PICTURE

The stove, the kettle, the tiles, the sink, the brass fitting, the countertop, the dish rack and its plates, the cabinets, the bucket, the walls, the window, the curtain, the flowerpot, the radiator, the table, the oilcloth and the parquet all stay exactly where they are, at the same size and in the same shape, from the first frame to the last. THEY are the clean stylized CGI cartoon render — even surfaces, soft rounded bevels, matte toy materials, gentle shadows — and they hold exactly the tone of the plate: the same lightness, the same gentle contrast, the same colour, one calm low-contrast look edge to edge.
THE MAN AND ALL THE WATER BELONG TO THE PAINTED LAYER SITTING ON TOP OF THAT RENDER, and they are made of paint and paper rather than of surfaces and light.
The camera holds one fixed position, with no zoom, no pan, no tilt and no reframing.

NOTHING ABOUT THE WATER IS SEE-THROUGH. Nothing about it glints, sparkles or catches the light. Nothing in the room reflects in it. It shows no depth, no thickness and no rounding: it is flat colour with a cut edge. Its edges are straight-sided and torn, never rounded and never bulging.
IT MOVES AS A SMALL NUMBER OF HELD DRAWINGS. Each drawing sits still on screen, then the next drawing replaces it on one frame with nothing drawn in between. It is a sequence of separate pictures, on twos, not a continuous flow.

THE PIECES OF WATER, AND WHAT EACH ONE IS

ONE — THE FOUNTAIN over the brass fitting. One tall blue shape standing up out of the fitting, widening towards its top into a splayed crown, with a handful of separate white shapes laid across the crown and a few loose flat chips of white and blue hanging in the air beside it, each chip its own unconnected piece. It keeps the same height and the same width in every frame. Only the white shapes inside its silhouette swap for other white shapes, and the loose chips vanish and are replaced by other chips.

TWO — THE BLUE IN THE BASIN, AND IT RISES. One flat blue shape filling the bowl, with the white foam clusters as separate white shapes sitting on top of it. It is a little below the rim at the start; then level with the rim; then standing slightly proud of it, humped a fraction above the edge. Each of those levels is a held drawing, replaced by the next in one step. The foam rides up with it.

THREE — IT GOES OVER ON EVERY SIDE OF THE SINK. The bowl spills over ALL FOUR of its edges at once, not down one side only:
— over the NEAR edge, towards the camera, down the front of the cabinet below;
— over the FAR edge, at the back, against the tiled wall;
— over the edge on the STOVE SIDE, towards the left of the picture;
— over the edge on the DISH RACK SIDE, towards the right of the picture.
Each of those four is its own separate flat blue band with a torn edge down each side and a few white flecks on it, and each is joined at its top to the blue in the bowl. They ring the sink so that blue shows all the way round its rim.

FOUR — THE COUNTERTOP IS UNDER WATER. The blue that goes over the far edge and the two side edges spreads out and lies flat across the countertop as ONE BROAD FLAT BLUE SHAPE covering it, its torn outline running around the counter and up to the tiles at the back. The dish rack stands in it. That shape grows across the shot together with everything else, until most of the counter is blue.

FIVE — THE SHEET DOWN TO THE FLOOR, AND IT REACHES THE BOARDS. The band going over the near edge, and the blue running off the counter at the stove-side end, come DOWN THE WHOLE WAY TO THE FLOOR. Each is one long even-width blue band whose top touches the counter and whose bottom touches the boards, with nothing hanging free at either end. Down at the bottom each one opens out a little wider and its edge tears into the shape of the pool. They keep their width and their length in every frame; only their torn side edges swap for other torn edges. They never narrow, never break into pieces and never gather into a drip or a blob.

SIX — THE POOL ON THE FLOOR. One flat blue shape lying on the parquet, with a torn leading edge and a ragged line of separate white flecks laid along that edge. It is a piece of blue paper lying on the boards.

HOW THE POOL GROWS — SEPARATE HELD SHAPES, NOT A CREEPING LIQUID

The pool is redrawn a few times across the shot, and each redraw is A BIGGER PIECE OF BLUE PAPER THAN THE ONE BEFORE, covering more of the floor.
Each of those shapes is HELD STILL on screen for a stretch of time, and then the next, larger one replaces it in a single step. Between one shape and the next nothing is drawn: the edge does not travel, it is simply somewhere further out on the next held drawing.
Each new shape CONTAINS THE WHOLE OF THE ONE BEFORE IT: the floor that was blue stays blue, and only the outline reaches further.
The shapes in order cover: the boards at the foot of the cabinet; then out across the herringbone parquet; then round the yellow bucket, closing on both sides so the bucket stands in the blue; then up to the big blue slipper on his straight leg; then around both his slippers and along the hem of his trousers, with white flecks where the blue meets his painted shapes.
IN THE LAST FRAME THE POOL IS AT ITS BIGGEST AND THE TAP IS STILL POURING. The picture ends in the middle of the flood with no sign of it easing.

EVERYTHING RISES TOGETHER

The fountain plays at exactly the same height and the same width in the last frame as in the first: as much comes in at the end as at the beginning.
THE BOWL, THE FOUR BANDS OVER THE RIM, THE SHEET OF WATER ON THE COUNTERTOP, THE BANDS DOWN TO THE FLOOR AND THE POOL ALL STEP UP TOGETHER, on the same held drawings and in the same rhythm. When the pool is redrawn bigger, the counter is redrawn wetter and the bowl is redrawn higher on that same frame.
So the chain always reads whole, from top to bottom: the fountain, the bowl brimming over on every side, the flooded counter, the bands down to the floor, the pool. Each one touches the next.
All of it is already running before the first frame, and nothing about it eases off by the last.

HE DOES NOT MOVE, AND THAT IS THE JOKE

He holds the exact drawing he has in the first frame, from the first frame to the last: the same lopsided arrangement, the same limbs in the same places, the same flat chartreuse green skin, olive hair and moustache, the two black X marks, the wine-red tongue hanging out sideways, the half-off slipper hanging on his toes. Not a digit moves, not a shrug, not a breath, not a twitch when the water arrives. He is a painted cut-out lying on the floor and the flood happens around him.
He keeps the same size on screen and the same painted surface throughout. His painted shadows are fixed graphic shapes attached to the artwork.

Under the blue: the countertop, the foot of the dish rack, the front of the cabinet under the sink, the boards of the kitchen floor, the rug, the foot of the bucket, and the lower parts of his slippers and trousers.
Clear of it: the stove, the kettle, the tiles above the counter, the window, the flowerpot, the radiator, the table and its oilcloth.

The stove, the kettle, the tiles, the sink, the brass fitting, the countertop, the dish rack and its plates, the cabinets, the bucket, the walls, the window, the curtain, the flowerpot, the radiator, the table, the oilcloth and the parquet all stay exactly where they are, at the same size and in the same shape, from the first frame to the last. TASK
A small old apartment kitchen, warm and bright and cared-for, belonging to a neighbour woman. It is empty of people. Built as a stylized CGI cartoon set.

HOW IT IS MADE — THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PART
Everything in this picture is a stylized CGI cartoon render, built the way a toy or a diorama is built:
GEOMETRY IS CHUNKY AND SIMPLIFIED. Every object is reduced to its clearest big shapes, with a few large forms rather than many small details. Nothing is finely modelled.
EVERY EDGE IS SOFTLY ROUNDED with a generous bevel, so that no corner in the picture is sharp. The counter, the cabinet doors, the window frame, the table, the shelves, the pots — all of them have soft rounded edges that catch a gentle highlight.
EVERY MATERIAL IS MATTE AND TOY-LIKE: even, smooth, slightly soft, like painted wood or moulded plastic. The wood reads as painted rather than grained, the plaster as smooth rather than rough, the metal as dull rather than mirrored.
THE SHADING IS SOFT AND SIMPLE: broad gentle gradients across each surface, soft raytraced shadows with no hard edges, and no complicated reflections anywhere.
The whole thing looks handmade and inviting, closer to a doll's house room than to a photograph.

THE CAMERA
Three-quarter view into the room from the open side, standing height, lens level with a slight tilt down, about 35 mm. The sink with its brass tap sits near the middle of the frame and is the anchor everything else is placed around. The room reads as a place to stand in, with depth and with two walls visible.

THE ROOM
A small old apartment kitchen. A run of counter along the back wall with a white ceramic sink and a brass tap; a small gas stove beside it with a kettle and an enamel pot; wooden cabinets below the counter with brass handles; plain tiles on the wall above it. ONE WINDOW ON THE RIGHT with a radiator beneath it and light curtains drawn back. A fridge at the LEFT. A small table with a warm cream tablecloth standing by the window wall, with two stools and a bowl of fruit on it. A parquet floor in warm honey wood.

WHAT MAKES IT HERS
WOODEN SHELVES on the wall above the counter, two of them, plain planks on small brackets, crowded with SMALL GLASS SPICE JARS with metal lids — a row of them in different sizes, filled with things in reds, ochres, browns and greens.
LIVING PLANTS: a fat leafy one in a terracotta pot on the windowsill, a trailing one in a hanging pot near the window with its leaves coming down, and a small pot of herbs on the counter. They are healthy and green and there are enough of them to notice.
A STRING OF ONIONS hanging beside the shelves. A wooden spoon standing in a jar by the hob. A folded cloth on the counter rail.
Everything is tidy, everything has a place, and the whole room reads as somebody's home.

THE LIGHT
One source: warm daylight coming in through the window on the RIGHT, so all shadows fall to the LEFT and all of them agree. The room is BRIGHT and the light is generous — it reaches into the corners and every part of the picture keeps its detail. Shadows are soft, warm and shallow. The window is the brightest thing in the picture and nothing else is blown out.

# ACTION TIMING

## 0.0–3.5s — COOKING / GROOVE / ANTICIPATION

NO WATER FALLS.

Camera completely locked.

The woman casually cooks while keeping time with cheerful radio music.

Her RIGHT hand performs slow, simple stirring strokes with the wooden spoon.

Her feet remain planted.

Her groove is intentionally minimal and readable:

**beat → small knee dip → tiny alternating hip accent → settle → hold.**

The next beat mirrors the accent to the opposite side.

Her shoulders follow the body subtly.

The dress hem and shoulder towel settle slightly after each body accent.

No walking.

No foot sliding.

No body rotation toward camera.

At approximately **2.5s**, she taps the wooden spoon once against the pan rim.

Meanwhile, above her:

the ceiling stain slowly darkens and expands.

By approximately **3.3s**, one tiny circular bead is visibly hanging beneath the stain.

---

## 3.5s — FIRST DROP / COMEDIC HIT

The single hanging bead detaches.

It falls vertically down the locked x≈53% corridor.

It passes through open air in front of the white extractor hood.

It lands clearly on the grey-teal towel on her screen-left shoulder.

A tiny dark wet mark appears on the towel and remains.

One distinct soft **tap** is heard.

---

## 3.5–5.0s — FREEZE

The woman stops immediately.

Her body freezes.

The spoon stops inside the pan.

Her feet remain planted.

No second drop falls.

The pause is important.

Only:

- frying oil continues sizzling
- flat painted steam continues rising
- radio continues playing

Hold the comedic silence in her body.

---

## 5.0–7.0s — REALIZATION

Still facing away from camera, she slowly tilts her head backward to inspect the ceiling.

The motion happens in the flat 2D picture plane.

The crown of her head rolls slightly toward camera while the curlers point upward.

The BACK of her head remains toward camera.

Her face remains completely hidden.

Her LEFT hand leaves her hip and touches the damp patch on the towel.

She holds her fingers against it.

Emotion:

**puzzled and mildly annoyed, not frightened.**

Feet remain planted.

No water falls during the beginning of this reaction.

---

## 7.0–9.0s — DRIPPING BEGINS

The same ceiling stain produces:

one second bead,

then one third bead,

then one fourth bead.

Approximately one drop per second.

Each bead:

- originates from exactly the same ceiling point
- has exactly the same circular shape
- has exactly the same size
- travels down exactly the same narrow vertical corridor

The drops contact the localized shoulder/curlers area.

The towel's wet patch becomes slightly darker and wider.

The ceiling stain becomes somewhat wider and darker.

The woman keeps her head tilted upward and her left hand touching her shoulder.

She does not dodge.

She does not turn around.

## 9.0–12.0s — ACCELERATING DRIP

The SAME leak begins releasing drops progressively faster.

Frequency increases smoothly:

approximately 1 drop/sec →

2 drops/sec →

approaching 3 drops/sec by the final second.

The drop SIZE does not increase.

The leak WIDTH does not increase.

Only the DROP FREQUENCY increases.

All beads remain confined to the same narrow x≈53% corridor.

Impacts remain concentrated around:

- towel
- nearby curlers
- narrow near edge of stovetop

Occasional runoff reaches the one small wet patch between her slippers.

When a drop reaches the hot stovetop edge:

a tiny brief steam hiss.

The woman holds her puzzled pose:

head tilted upward,

left hand touching the wet shoulder,

right hand still holding the spoon,

back toward camera.

The dripping rate is still accelerating on the FINAL FRAME.

Do not resolve the situation.

HOW HE LIES, FROM THE FIRST FRAME
He is already on the floor in the first frame, on the open parquet in front of the stove, and this is his drawing for the whole shot.
HE IS DOWN ON HIS BACK. His head is at the stove, tipped back with his face turned up and his olive hair against the white enamel of the oven door. His shoulders and his back are on the boards at the foot of the stove.
HIS BODY RUNS OUT FROM THERE TOWARDS THE RIGHT of the picture, along the open floor.
ONE LEG IS BENT WITH THE KNEE UP; the other is stretched out full length along the boards towards the lower right, its slipper fallen over on its side.
HIS ARMS LIE OUT ON THE FLOOR to either side of him, open, the digits loose and apart.
He holds that exact arrangement until she takes hold of him, and no part of him rearranges itself.

WHERE SHE COMES IN — FROM THE LEFT
She is out of the picture at the start, off past the LEFT-HAND EDGE of the frame, beyond the fridge.
SHE COMES IN FROM BEHIND THAT LEFT EDGE, already running, and she is drawn as A FEW HELD POSITIONS ACROSS THE FLOOR rather than a smooth run: her leading shoulder clears the edge, then she is a third of the way in, then two thirds, then she has arrived. Each of those sits still for a beat and the next replaces it in a single step.
SHE ARRIVES BESIDE HIM, in front of the stove and to the left of his head, and stops hard, her weight going forward and the hem of her gown swinging on a beat after her.
Then she drops to her knees beside his head and leans in over his shoulders. She is SEEN IN THREE-QUARTER VIEW FROM BEHIND AND TO THE SIDE — her shoulder and the side of her face towards us, her curlers in silhouette, her back and the wide fall of the gown reading clearly. She stays at that angle for the rest of the shot.
SHE STAYS ON THE LEFT-HAND SIDE OF THE PICTURE THROUGHOUT: she never crosses over him and never moves round to the other side.

THE SHAKE — THREE OF THEM, AND THEY ARE COUNTABLE
She takes him by BOTH SHOULDERS, one hand on each, gripping the heavy part of him where his sleeves meet his neck.
THERE ARE EXACTLY THREE SHAKES, and each is one clean move with a hard stop and a held beat after it.
EACH SHAKE IS THE SAME SHAPE: she pulls his shoulders up off the floor towards herself, and lets them drop back. The travel is short — his shoulders lift about the width of his own head and come straight back down. It is a firm tug, not a rattle, and nothing about him whips or blurs.
BETWEEN THE SHAKES SHE HOLDS COMPLETELY STILL, gripping him, for a beat. Those held beats are as long as the shakes themselves.
HIS HEAD IS THE ONE THING THAT LAGS. It is its own flat painted piece hinged at his neck: when his shoulders come up it stays behind and tips back against the stove, when his shoulders drop it comes down after them and settles a beat late. Its size on screen stays exactly the same through all of it, and it hinges rather than stretching.
His arms, his hips, his bent knee, his straight leg and his slippers stay exactly where they lie: the shaking reaches his shoulders and his head and goes no further down his body.
His painted face keeps its X marks and its lolling tongue in every frame and nothing about it changes.

WHAT HAPPENS
First: the kitchen and the man on the floor, held still for a beat, exactly as the first frame has them.
Then: SHE COMES IN FROM THE LEFT, three or four held positions across the floor, and stops hard beside him.
Then: SHE DROPS TO HER KNEES, three held drawings, and takes him by both shoulders.
Then: SHAKE ONE — up, drop, hold. SHAKE TWO — up, drop, hold. SHAKE THREE — up, drop, hold.
Finally: she stays kneeling, still holding his shoulders, looking down at his face, and the picture holds like that to the last frame. He lies exactly as he did.

THEY ARE PAINTINGS ON GLASS
Both of them are flat painted images lying on glass in front of the render: an outline and a fill, with no thickness and no volume. Each frame of each of them is an individually painted drawing, and their construction and proportions stay identical from drawing to drawing. Their colours stay their own flat painted colours whatever the room does around them, and they stay outside the room's lighting entirely: no shine, no reflection and no shading from the room falls on either of them. Their painted shadows are fixed graphic shapes attached to their artwork, lying flat on the boards. All of their movement stays inside the flat plane of the picture. Each hand keeps four digits held together.
THEY ARE TWO SEPARATE DRAWINGS AND THEY STAY SEPARATE. Where she leans over him, her painted shape passes in front of his as a clean flat layer overlap with both outlines visible at the join. Her raspberry gown and his mint shirt keep their own edges and their own colours where they meet, and neither of them takes on any part of the other.

WHAT HOLDS
Every object of the kitchen stays exactly where the first image has it, at the same size and in the same shape, from the first frame to the last: the fridge, the cabinets, the counter, the bread box, the salt shaker, the bottle, the stove, the kettle, the sink, the tap, the pipe, the bucket, the dish rack, the tiled wall, the utensils, the parquet, the rug. The room holds exactly the plate's tone — the same lightness, the same gentle contrast, the same colour, one calm look edge to edge. The camera holds one fixed position, with no zoom, no pan, no tilt and no reframing. Exactly one woman and one man in the picture and nobody else appears. Her size on screen and his stay constant from the moment each is in frame.

Limited 2D animation on twos: strong readable held poses replaced in single steps, with very few drawings between them. Every move starts small, accelerates and snaps into the next pose with a hard stop. Between the poses everything sits completely still, and the holds are long.

FIRST — a short beat of stillness, no more than a moment: she kneels over him gripping his shoulders, he lies there green with his X marks and his tongue out.

The green goes and the living paint arrives at once: terracotta skin, ginger hair and moustache, navy stripes on white, open eyes with round dark pupils, the tongue gone back in. THEN — HE SITS UP AND GRABS HER, IMMEDIATELY. WHAT IS GOING ON INSIDE HER, AND HOW IT SHOWS
She has just been grabbed and kissed by a corpse and she is furious about it. She wants to be out of this flat immediately.
BUT SHE IS NOT GOING TO GIVE ANYONE THE SATISFACTION OF SEEING THAT. She is leaving with her dignity in one piece, and the whole performance is her holding herself together.
IT SHOWS IN HOW TIGHTLY SHE IS HELD, and nowhere else. Her back is very straight. Her shoulders are squared and pulled back. Her chin is up. Her hands are closed and pressed against her sides. Everything about her is a fraction too composed, too upright, too correct — the stiffness of somebody who has decided to walk out properly.
AND IT ALMOST BREAKS. Her walk is a shade quicker than a dignified walk should be, and her steps are a little too even, as though she is counting them. Once or twice her stride nearly runs away with her before she takes it back. That flicker between fleeing and marching is the shot.
NOTHING ABOUT HER IS THEATRICAL: she does not stamp, does not gesture, does not shake and does not hurry openly. It is all in the tightness of the hold.

SHE IS ALREADY IN THE PICTURE when the shot opens. She stands in the hall, DEEPER IN THE ROOM AND A LITTLE TO THE LEFT of the open doorway, on the boards with her back to camera, already squared up and facing the door, about to go. Her face is out of the picture at the start; what we read is her straight back, her curlers, the wide fall of her gown and her slippers.
Because she is deep in the hall she is small in the frame, and she stays that size for the whole shot: her feet stay on the same patch of boards and she never comes towards camera or goes away from it.
THE BASIN LIES ON THE FLOOR AHEAD OF HER, between where she stands and the open door.

The dead man takes the neighbour. One continuous take: she comes down to him to see whether he is dead, he wakes under her hand and pulls her into him, she gives in, and the tap bursts over them.

Primary event: she lowers herself onto the floor beside his chest and settles there, her body held back away from him.
End state: she kneels on the parquet at the LEFT, level with his chest, her body leaning back, her painted face toward the viewer, her left fist tight on the slipper down by her hip, her right hand free at her side.

[Stage 2]
Continue from the previous stage: he lies unchanged in the same sprawl, head at the right; she kneels at the left with the slipper at her hip.
Primary event: her free right hand goes out and pats his cheek twice, light and quick.
End state: her right hand rests on his green cheek, her arm reaching out across his chest, and it stays there.

[Stage 3]
Continue from the previous stage: her hand rests on his cheek, her fist on the slipper down at her hip, he lies in the same sprawl.
Primary event: he comes alive under her hand — his tongue slides back into his mouth and the mouth closes, the two black X marks come off his eyes so his open eyes are there underneath, and the terracotta runs through him in one pass from his head at the right along his body to his feet at the left, his ginger colour arriving in his hair and moustache as it passes.
End state: he lies in the exact same sprawl, in the same place in the frame, now terracotta with ginger hair and moustache, his mouth closed and his open eyes looking up. [Stage 4]
Continue from the previous stage: he is alive and sprawled as before, her hand on his cheek, her fist on the slipper.

[Stage 5]
Continue from the previous stage: the two of them are locked together, his arm round her back, her slipper hand at her hip.

[Stage 6]
Continue from the previous stage: the two of them are locked together, her hand flat on his chest.
Primary event: his arm draws her further down and back, tipping her over across him in one long slow bend, the way it is done in old films, and at the moment the bend arrives the tap bursts off-screen and a column of water rises above them.
End state: she is tipped back across him, the two of them held together, and a blue-teal column of water pours down over them from above.

[Stage 7]
Continue from the previous stage: they are locked together, tipped back, the water pouring.
